title: Top 10 UX Misunderstandings
intro: These misunderstandings sound just enough like truth to pass a design review. Each one hides complexity instead of handling it — and shifts work onto the user.

learn.title: Navigation, clicks, and progressive disclosure
learn.text:
**"Search or AI can fix bad navigation."**
Search and chatbots are additional access paths, not replacements. Baymard found about half of ecommerce users prefer search, half use navigation. You need both.

**"Optimize for fewer clicks."**
The three-click rule is built on flimsy data. A click with **strong information scent** (users can predict where it leads) is cheap. A click into uncertainty is expensive — even if it's the first one.

TurboTax has more clicks than a single tax form. It's a better experience.

**"Progressive disclosure simplifies everything."**
Hiding information doesn't simplify — it just moves complexity. Progressive disclosure works for secondary or advanced content. It breaks when you hide **decision-critical** information.

Never hide: eligibility rules, consequences, fees, destructive-action warnings, or permission impacts.

right.label: Reality
items: Search supplements navigation — you need both
Show decision-critical info at the moment of decision

try.q: A designer hides pricing caveats in a tooltip to keep the page "clean." What's wrong with this?
options: Pricing information is decision-critical and should be visible at the moment of decision
Tooltips don't work on mobile so it's a technical issue
The page should show all information at once
Caveats should be on a separate page
try.explain: Decision-critical information should never be hidden behind progressive disclosure. Fees, caveats, and constraints need to be visible when users make the choice.

learn.title: Forms, validation, and filtering
learn.text:
**"Simpler forms = fewer labels."**
A form is simple when users complete it with low uncertainty, low memory load, and low recovery effort. Looking clean isn't the same thing.

Baymard found inline labels cause users to **delete their own input** just to see the label again. Placeholder text makes it harder to remember, check, and fix entries.

**"Validation = blocking bad input."**
Validation should help users **recover**, not just block them. Show the problem near its source, explain it in plain language, preserve user work, and confirm success when it helps.

A generic "Invalid input" is not validation.

**"Filters are nice-to-haves."**
For many tasks, filters and sorting are the **primary** way users manage information. This applies beyond ecommerce — admin consoles, CRMs, audit logs, security events. Design filters around user mental models, not database structure.

left.label: Don't
items: Clear the form on failed submission

right.label: Do
items: Show specific errors near the field
Preserve all entered data on failure
Design filters around how users think

try.q: A payment form clears all fields when a credit card is declined. What principle does this violate?
options: Validation should preserve user work and help them recover
Forms should never clear
Credit card validation should always happen on the server side
Payment forms should have fewer fields
try.explain: Clearing a form on failed submission is a major usability failure. Validation should respect the effort users already invested and help them fix just the problem.

learn.title: Icons, hover, and sample size
learn.text:
**"Icons are self-explanatory."**
Teams become fluent in their own product language. Users don't. Very few icons are broadly recognized — a trash can works, but "reconcile variance" does not.

**Label all icons.** For usability, accessibility, and code compliance.

**"Fast hover menus feel responsive."**
Hair-trigger hover (no delay) feels jumpy. Baymard recommends a 300–500ms delay to reduce flicker and accidental triggers. And hover-only patterns exclude touch, keyboard, and assistive technology users.

When in doubt, don't hide it under a hover.

**"Small samples = invalid findings."**
Sample size should follow the study goal. 5 users reveal common usability problems. 50+ users are needed for benchmarking, rare issues, or precise estimates.

A researcher reporting a clear pattern from 12 users shouldn't be dismissed — but shouldn't claim statistical precision either.

right.label: Reality
items: Label all icons — team fluency ≠ user fluency
Match sample to the claim you're making

try.q: A stakeholder says: "12 participants isn't enough to prove anything." How should you respond?
options: 12 users can reveal common patterns
They're right
Small studies are always invalid
Show them the p-value from your analysis
try.explain: Small formative studies suit identifying common problems. Larger samples are for benchmarking and precise estimates. The key is matching sample to claim. (Match sample size to the study goal.)

test.q: According to Baymard research, about what proportion of ecommerce users prefer search over main navigation?
options: About half — both are essential
Almost all users prefer search
Less than 10% use search
It depends entirely on the product category
test.explain: Baymard found roughly half preferred search and half used navigation. Both are essential access paths — one can't replace the other.

test.q: What does "information scent" mean in navigation design?
options: Users' ability to predict where a link will lead based on its label and context
How many clicks it takes to reach content
The visual prominence of navigation elements
The loading speed of each page in the path
test.explain: Information scent is about predictability. Users scan labels and context to decide if a path will lead where they want. Clear scent makes even longer paths feel easy.

test.q: Why do inline (placeholder) labels cause usability problems?
options: Users delete their input to see the label again, increasing memory load and errors
They make forms look too simple
Screen readers can't detect them
They only render correctly in specific browsers, which makes forms inconsistent across devices
test.explain: Baymard found users delete their own input to re-read disappeared labels. Placeholder text increases memory load and makes it harder to check and fix entries.

test.q: What delay does Baymard recommend for hover-triggered dropdown menus?
options: 300–500 milliseconds
No delay — instant response
1–2 seconds
50–100 milliseconds
test.explain: Baymard recommends 300–500ms to prevent flicker and accidental triggers. This is a well-documented issue that persisted in testing for over a decade.

test.q: When should you use progressive disclosure?
options: For secondary or advanced content — never for decision-critical information
Always — it makes every interface simpler
For all form fields to reduce visual clutter
For pricing and fee information, so that users aren't overwhelmed at the moment of choice
test.explain: Progressive disclosure works for rarely used or advanced features. Never hide eligibility rules, consequences, fees, warnings, or permission impacts.
